t: Minimum Number of Coins to be Added
o: Classic 'patching array': with a multiset of coins, if every value in [1, reach] is obtainable, adding a coin of value c ≤ reach+1 extends coverage to [1, reach+c]; if the next sorted coin exceeds reach+1, a gap at reach+1 forces us to add a coin worth exactly reach+1. Repeat until reach ≥ target.
k: Invariant: after processing some coins, all of [1, reach] is obtainable.
A sorted coin c with c ≤ reach+1 safely extends reach to reach+c; c > reach+1 means reach+1 is unreachable and must be patched.
Each added coin doubles-plus-one the reach, so the count of additions is O(log target).

a.i: Sort coins. Maintain reach = 0. If the next coin ≤ reach+1, absorb it (reach += coin). Otherwise insert a virtual coin of value reach+1 (reach += reach+1, count++). Stop when reach ≥ target. Optimality: reach+1 is the smallest uncovered value, and no arrangement of existing coins can cover it without a coin ≤ reach+1, so adding exactly reach+1 is both necessary and maximal.
s: Sort coins; reach = 0, added = 0, pointer i = 0.
While reach < target: if i < len and coins[i] <= reach+1, reach += coins[i++]; else added++, reach += reach+1.
a.t: O(n log n + log target) — sorting plus at most logarithmically many patches

w: This is the canonical Patching Array proof — practice stating the exchange argument crisply. Pitfall: use 64-bit reach since patches double it and target can be 10^5 (safe here, but habit matters). Edge cases: coins missing 1 entirely, target already covered by coins alone.
